# Hillary Clinton’s Move to the State Department: Confirmation, Clinton Foundation Questions, and the Fight to Fill Her Senate Seat

When President Barack Obama chose Hillary Rodham Clinton to be secretary of state, the decision brought together two former rivals at a pivotal moment in American politics. Clinton, who had battled Obama through a long and bruising 2008 Democratic primary campaign, became one of the most prominent members of his new Cabinet and the face of his administration’s foreign policy.

Her nomination also set off a chain of political and procedural events: a Senate confirmation process complicated by concerns over former President Bill Clinton’s global charitable work, and an intense scramble in New York over who would inherit Clinton’s U.S. Senate seat.

## From primary rival to Cabinet nominee

Obama announced Clinton as his choice for secretary of state in December 2008 as he assembled a “team of rivals” after winning the presidency. The selection was widely seen as both pragmatic and symbolic. Clinton brought star power, international experience, and relationships with foreign leaders built during her years as first lady and senator. For Obama, appointing her helped unify the Democratic Party after a divisive primary season.

For Clinton, the post offered a new role on the world stage. She had represented New York in the Senate since 2001 and had become one of the best-known politicians in the country. As secretary of state, she would succeed Condoleezza Rice and take charge of diplomacy during a period marked by wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, concerns over Iran’s nuclear program, tensions with Russia, and the global financial crisis.

## The Senate confirmation process

Cabinet nominees are subject to Senate confirmation, and Clinton’s nomination went before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. In ordinary circumstances, a senator nominated to the Cabinet often receives a smooth confirmation, especially when the nominee has strong relationships with colleagues from both parties. Clinton’s stature and long Senate service gave her significant bipartisan support.

Her confirmation hearing focused on broad foreign policy questions: the future of the Iraq War, strategy in Afghanistan and Pakistan, relations with Iran and North Korea, human rights, global development, and the role of diplomacy in restoring America’s standing abroad. Clinton emphasized “smart power,” a phrase that came to define her early approach—combining diplomacy, development, economic tools, and military strength.

The Foreign Relations Committee approved her nomination, but the full Senate vote was briefly delayed because of Republican concerns about possible conflicts of interest involving Bill Clinton’s foundation and speaking engagements. Ultimately, the Senate confirmed her on January 21, 2009, the day after Obama’s inauguration, by a vote of 94–2. She resigned from the Senate and was sworn in as the 67th secretary of state.

## Objections over Bill Clinton’s foundation

The chief complication surrounding Clinton’s nomination was not her own record but her husband’s post-presidential activities. Since leaving office, Bill Clinton had built the William J. Clinton Foundation into a major international philanthropic organization, with projects and donors around the world. The foundation worked on issues such as HIV/AIDS treatment, climate change, economic development, and public health.

Republican senators and ethics watchdogs raised concerns that foreign governments, corporations, or wealthy individuals might donate to the foundation while Hillary Clinton was secretary of state, potentially creating the appearance of influence over U.S. foreign policy. Bill Clinton’s paid speeches abroad also drew scrutiny, particularly if he were paid by entities with interests before the State Department.

To address these concerns, the Obama transition team and the Clintons negotiated a memorandum of understanding. Under the agreement, the foundation agreed to disclose its donors, including many past contributors, and to provide more transparency going forward. Bill Clinton also agreed to submit future paid speaking engagements and certain foundation activities to State Department ethics review. The foundation said it would restrict or review foreign government donations to reduce potential conflicts.

These steps satisfied most senators, though not all. Some Republicans argued that the safeguards did not go far enough and that the foundation’s global donor network would remain a potential ethical problem. Still, the objections were not enough to derail the nomination, and Clinton won overwhelming confirmation.

## The New York Senate succession battle

Clinton’s move to the State Department created a political prize in New York: an open U.S. Senate seat. Under New York law at the time, the governor had the power to appoint a replacement who would serve until a special election. That decision fell to Governor David Paterson, who had become governor in 2008 after Eliot Spitzer resigned.

The search quickly became a public spectacle. A long list of possible successors emerged, including Attorney General Andrew Cuomo, several members of Congress, and other prominent New York Democrats. But the most famous name was Caroline Kennedy, the daughter of President John F. Kennedy.

Kennedy’s interest drew enormous media attention. Supporters argued that she carried the Kennedy family legacy, had strong ties to Obama, and could raise money and command national attention. Critics countered that she had little electoral experience and gave uneven public interviews while trying to make her case. Her potential appointment became controversial, and she eventually withdrew from consideration, citing personal reasons.

Paterson ultimately chose Representative Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat from upstate New York, to fill Clinton’s seat. Gillibrand was less nationally known than Kennedy or Cuomo, but she had won a Republican-leaning House district and was viewed as someone who could broaden the Democratic Party’s appeal beyond New York City. Her appointment surprised many observers and immediately reshaped New York politics.

Gillibrand later won the special election and subsequent full terms, becoming one of the state’s two long-serving senators.

## A defining early move for the Obama administration

Hillary Clinton’s confirmation as secretary of state was one of the most consequential appointments of Obama’s first term. It elevated a former political rival into a central governing role and signaled Obama’s desire to bring experienced, high-profile figures into his administration.

The episode also foreshadowed issues that would follow Clinton for years: scrutiny of the Clinton Foundation, questions about political access and ethics, and the intense public attention surrounding every stage of her career. At the same time, it opened a new chapter in New York politics with Gillibrand’s appointment and rise in the Senate.

Clinton entered the State Department with broad bipartisan support, significant diplomatic challenges, and the unusual burden of managing not only her own public role but also the global political footprint of the Clinton family.

The Senate confirmed Clinton by a **94–2 roll-call vote**, with only two Republicans — **Sen. Jim DeMint of South Carolina** and **Sen. David Vitter of Louisiana** — voting against her nomination. The vote cleared the way for Clinton to assume control of the State Department at a moment when the incoming Obama administration faced wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, rising tensions with Iran, a fragile Middle East peace process and strained relations with key allies.

Clinton’s confirmation had been widely expected, but it was delayed briefly after some Republicans sought additional assurances about financial disclosures and foreign donations connected to the William J. Clinton Foundation. The foundation had agreed to disclose contributors and take other steps intended to limit conflicts while Clinton served as secretary of state.

DeMint and Vitter said those safeguards did not go far enough.

DeMint argued that Clinton’s confirmation raised unresolved questions about foreign donors to her husband’s foundation and possible influence over U.S. foreign policy. Vitter also cited concerns about transparency and potential conflicts of interest, saying the Senate should not move forward without stronger restrictions and disclosures.

Most Republicans, however, joined Democrats in backing Clinton.

Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, then chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, said he still had reservations about the foundation arrangement but would support the nomination. Cornyn said Clinton had provided “a level of disclosure and transparency” that allowed the process to move ahead, while adding that senators would continue to watch the issue closely.

Sen. John McCain of Arizona, Clinton’s former Senate colleague and Obama’s 2008 Republican presidential opponent, strongly supported her nomination. McCain praised Clinton’s qualifications and urged Republicans not to block the incoming president’s national security team, saying Obama was entitled to have his chosen advisers in place.

McCain described Clinton as well prepared for the role and said that, despite political differences, she had earned bipartisan respect in the Senate.

Clinton’s confirmation marked one of the most high-profile appointments in Obama’s Cabinet. A former first lady and two-term senator from New York, Clinton had battled Obama through a long and often bitter Democratic primary campaign before endorsing him and campaigning for him in the general election.

At the State Department, Clinton was expected to play a central role in implementing Obama’s pledge to restore U.S. alliances and emphasize diplomacy after the Bush administration years. Her appointment also placed one of the Democratic Party’s most recognizable figures in charge of America’s foreign policy agenda.

With the oath administered by Judge Oberly and the Senate vote complete, Clinton formally assumed office and prepared to address State Department employees as the new administration began its first full days in power.
